rows.india: Still common nationally; taught as a leading cause of mitral stenosis in young adults.
rows.australia: Rare overall but very high in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (21 for some).

rows.india: Often treat each risk factor (BP, cholesterol, glucose) against its own threshold.
rows.australia: Treatment is guided by absolute CVD risk using the Australian risk calculator, with assessment starting earlier for First Nations people.

rows.india: Fibrinolysis is common where PCI is not available; streptokinase may still be used.
rows.australia: Primary PCI within 90 minutes if possible. If PCI can't happen within 120 minutes (common rurally), give tenecteplase, sometimes pre-hospital.

rows.india: Cholesterol and glucose in mg/dL.
rows.australia: Lipids and glucose in mmol/L; troponin as high-sensitivity ng/L. Convert your reference ranges.

rows.india: TB is high on the list for everyone; sputum testing under NTEP.
rows.australia: TB is uncommon and mostly in people born overseas. Think TB in migrants and international students; state TB services manage it and it is notifiable.

rows.india: Empirical co-amoxiclav, cephalosporins, macrolides or fluoroquinolones are common.
rows.australia: Per eTG: mild, oral amoxicillin and/or doxycycline; moderate, IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline. Fluoroquinolones are not routine first line.

rows.india: Salbutamol (sometimes oral) and theophylline/deriphyllin are still used; ICS may be underused.
rows.australia: Australian Asthma Handbook: SABA-only treatment is not recommended in adults. Use an ICS-containing regimen, e.g. as-needed budesonide-formoterol. Written action plan.

rows.aspect: Main causes of COPD and lung disease
rows.india: Smoking plus biomass smoke exposure, especially in women.
rows.australia: Mainly smoking; spirometry confirms diagnosis (COPD-X). High mesothelioma rates from past asbestos use; lung cancer screening program for high-risk smokers.

rows.india: Treated under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Program, often by specialists.
rows.australia: DAAs are PBS-listed without disease-stage restriction; GPs routinely treat and cure HCV.

rows.india: Common in the general population.
rows.australia: Concentrated in people born in Asia-Pacific countries and First Nations people; screen these groups and monitor long term.

rows.india: No national program; colonoscopy mainly for symptoms.
rows.australia: National Bowel Cancer Screening Program: free iFOBT every 2 years, mailed at 50-74, requestable from 45. Positive test means colonoscopy.

rows.india: Amoebic liver abscess, typhoid, hepatitis A/E and abdominal TB are common.
rows.australia: These are mostly travel-related. Alcohol and fatty liver disease (MASLD) dominate chronic liver disease.

rows.india: Glucose in mg/dL (e.g. fasting 126 mg/dL).
rows.australia: Glucose in mmol/L (fasting 7.0 mmol/L); HbA1c 6.5% or 48 mmol/mol diagnoses diabetes.

rows.india: Opportunistic, or population screening from 30 under the NCD program.
rows.australia: AUSDRISK from age 40 in general, and from 18 in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, who get diabetes more often and younger.

rows.india: Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors and fixed-dose combinations are common, partly on cost.
rows.australia: SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 agonists favoured with CVD, heart failure or CKD. PBS criteria apply. Supplies via NDSS.

rows.india: Iodine-deficiency goitre is classic; universal salt iodisation.
rows.australia: Iodised salt in bread since 2009; pregnant and breastfeeding women are advised an iodine supplement (150 mcg daily).

rows.india: Creatinine in mg/dL.
rows.australia: Creatinine in umol/L; eGFR (CKD-EPI) reported automatically; albuminuria as urine albumin:creatinine ratio (uACR).

rows.india: Diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, and CKD of unknown cause in some regions.
rows.australia: Diabetes and hypertension lead. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have far higher kidney failure rates.

rows.india: Usually found when symptomatic or on routine tests.
rows.australia: Kidney Health Check (BP, eGFR, uACR) every 1-2 years for at-risk people in general practice.

rows.india: Cost is a major barrier; free dialysis in public hospitals under national schemes.
rows.australia: Publicly funded; home dialysis encouraged. Remote patients often have to relocate for dialysis, a real cultural and social burden.

rows.india: Thrombolysis mostly in tertiary centres; access is limited.
rows.australia: Stroke units and telestroke for rural hospitals. Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours; endovascular clot retrieval for large vessel occlusion.

rows.india: Rarely a formal part of management.
rows.australia: Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive' sets standards. The patient must notify the licensing authority; the doctor advises and documents.

rows.india: Neurocysticercosis is a common cause.
rows.australia: Neurocysticercosis is rare; think of it mainly in migrants. Standard epilepsy workup otherwise.

rows.india: Relatively uncommon.
rows.australia: More common, and prevalence rises with distance from the equator (highest in Tasmania).

rows.india: Haemoglobin in g/dL (7 g/dL).
rows.australia: Haemoglobin in g/L (70 g/L).

rows.india: Very common and often treated as nutritional; hookworm and thalassaemia trait considered.
rows.australia: Always find the cause. In men and postmenopausal women, investigate for GI blood loss (gastroscopy/colonoscopy) and test for coeliac disease.

rows.india: Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma.
rows.australia: Prothrombinex-VF plus vitamin K for major bleeding; FFP only if it is unavailable.

rows.india: Replacement donation by family is still common.
rows.australia: Unpaid volunteer donors via Lifeblood. Patient blood management: restrictive thresholds, generally Hb below 70 g/L in stable patients.

rows.india: Broad-spectrum agents (cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, carbapenems) are often first line, reflecting resistance and access.
rows.australia: Narrowest effective agent per eTG. Fluoroquinolones and carbapenems are restricted. Stewardship is examined.

rows.india: Malaria, dengue, typhoid, scrub typhus and leptospirosis are everyday local diagnoses.
rows.australia: Mostly acquired overseas. Always take a travel history, and exclude malaria urgently in a febrile returned traveller.

rows.india: Different endemic pattern.
rows.australia: Melioidosis (tropical north), Q fever (farm and abattoir workers), Ross River and Barmah Forest viruses, and Japanese encephalitis in some regions.

rows.india: Focus on testing and ART through NACO centres.
rows.australia: PrEP is PBS-subsidised; treatment as prevention (U=U) is standard messaging.

rows.india: Standard classification criteria for RA, SLE and gout.
rows.australia: Largely the same criteria and workup.

rows.india: Access limited mainly by cost.
rows.australia: PBS authority only after documented failure of conventional DMARDs and disease activity scores; usually rheumatologist-initiated.

rows.india: Urate target under 6 mg/dL.
rows.australia: Urate in mmol/L: target under 0.36 (under 0.30 with tophi). Start allopurinol low and titrate.

rows.india: Analgesics and NSAIDs are often the mainstay.
rows.australia: Exercise, weight loss and education first. Opioids are not recommended; arthroscopy is not for knee OA.

rows.india: Rare in darker skin types; little emphasis.
rows.australia: Very high rates; melanoma, BCC and SCC are daily GP work. Dermoscopy and GP excisions are expected skills.

rows.india: Refer to dermatology.
rows.australia: Excision biopsy with a narrow (about 2 mm) margin for suspected melanoma; don't shave or partially biopsy.

rows.india: Tinea (often with steroid-combination cream misuse), leprosy and scabies.
rows.australia: Leprosy is rare. Scabies and impetigo matter in remote communities. Use plain antifungals, no steroid combinations.

rows.india: Sun protection is not a public health focus.
rows.australia: SunSmart 'slip, slop, slap, seek, slide'. No national skin screening program; checks are targeted to higher-risk people.

rows.india: Family is usually the main carer; formal aged care is limited.
rows.australia: Most older people live independently. Government-funded home or residential care is accessed through My Aged Care and an aged care assessment.

rows.india: Rarely formalised; family often decides.
rows.australia: Advance care directives and appointed substitute decision-makers are expected. Titles and forms vary by state.

rows.india: Polypharmacy often not systematically reviewed.
rows.australia: Deprescribing is emphasised; GP can arrange a pharmacist Home Medicines Review. Falls risk assessment is routine.

rows.india: Recognised but rarely acted on formally.
rows.australia: Screen for and act on elder abuse; serious incidents in residential aged care must be reported under a national scheme.
000 (112 also works from mobiles).

rows.india: Big four snakes and polyvalent ASV; tourniquets or cutting the bite are still seen.
rows.australia: Pressure immobilisation bandage and splint, keep still, don't wash the bite. Monitor for coagulopathy; give antivenom if envenomed.

rows.india: Organophosphates, aluminium phosphide and paraquat.
rows.australia: Paracetamol, benzodiazepines and antidepressants. Use the Australian paracetamol guideline and Poisons Information 13 11 26.

rows.india: Varies by hospital.
rows.australia: Australasian Triage Scale, categories 1 to 5, each with a target time to be seen.

rows.india: Nimesulide, metamizole and many fixed-dose combinations are widely used.
rows.australia: Not available. Learn Australian names, e.g. paracetamol, adrenaline, frusemide/furosemide, glyceryl trinitrate. Check eTG and AMH.

rows.india: Antibiotics and many prescription drugs are often bought without a script.
rows.australia: Strict scheduling (S2, S3, S4, S8). Antibiotics are prescription only; codeine has been prescription-only since 2018.

rows.india: Brand names are common on prescriptions.
rows.australia: Prescribe by active ingredient; pharmacists may substitute brands. PBS subsidy, some needing authority approval.

rows.india: Tightly restricted under the NDPS Act, often under-prescribed.
rows.australia: Check real-time prescription monitoring before prescribing S8 drugs; rules and permits vary by state.

rows.india: Clinical diagnosis with ultrasound; surgery principles as taught.
rows.australia: Largely the same: appendicitis, cholecystitis and obstruction are diagnosed and managed similarly.

rows.india: Abdominal TB, amoebic liver abscess and typhoid perforation are common.
rows.australia: Rare, mainly in migrants or travellers. Hydatid disease can still occur in rural sheep-farming areas.

rows.india: Patient often goes directly to a surgeon.
rows.australia: GP refers. Public elective surgery waiting lists use urgency categories 1-3 (within 30, 90 or 365 days), or private care.

rows.india: Postoperative antibiotic courses of several days are common.
rows.australia: Single pre-incision dose (usually cefazolin) per eTG; prolonged postoperative courses are not recommended.

rows.india: ATLS principles.
rows.australia: Largely the same; taught as EMST (the RACS version of ATLS).

rows.india: Two-wheeler road crashes, falls and assault dominate.
rows.australia: Road trauma, farm injuries (quad bikes, machinery) and drowning are major themes.

rows.india: Patients travel or are referred to a tertiary centre.
rows.australia: Long-distance retrieval by the Royal Flying Doctor Service or state services, so stabilisation and packaging for transfer is examined.

rows.india: Register a medico-legal case (MLC) and inform police.
rows.australia: No MLC system; police are not automatically informed. Report certain deaths to the coroner; blood alcohol rules vary by state.

rows.india: Spinal TB (Pott's) and chronic osteomyelitis are common.
rows.australia: Spinal TB is rare. Staph aureus dominates; flucloxacillin or cefazolin per eTG.

rows.india: X-ray is often done routinely after injury.
rows.australia: Validated rules are expected: Ottawa ankle and knee rules, Canadian C-spine rule.

rows.india: Calcium and vitamin D; treatment often after fracture if affordable.
rows.australia: DXA-based PBS criteria (minimal-trauma fracture or qualifying T-score). Never stop denosumab without follow-on therapy (rebound fractures).

rows.india: Often ordered routinely in older men.
rows.australia: No screening program. Discuss benefits and harms (overdiagnosis, biopsy risks) before testing, and document the patient's decision.

rows.india: Fluoroquinolones or nitrofurantoin; high ESBL rates.
rows.australia: eTG: trimethoprim 3 days, nitrofurantoin 5 days or cefalexin 5 days. Fluoroquinolones not first line.

rows.india: Ultrasound and X-ray KUB.
rows.australia: Largely the same management; non-contrast CT KUB is standard, with medical expulsive therapy for small distal stones.

rows.india: Very common, often late presentation.
rows.australia: Much higher amputation rates in First Nations people. Regular foot checks, podiatry and high-risk foot services are expected.

rows.india: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's) gets heavy textbook emphasis.
rows.australia: Atherosclerosis is the usual cause; Buerger's is rare.

rows.india: Warfarin or acenocoumarol, often on cost grounds.
rows.australia: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are usually first line. Acenocoumarol is not available.

rows.india: No program.
rows.australia: No national program either; targeted ultrasound for higher-risk older people, e.g. older men who smoke.

rows.india: Antibiotics given routinely.
rows.australia: Most children get analgesia and watchful waiting. Antibiotics (amoxicillin) for infants, unwell children and First Nations children.

rows.india: Antibiotics very commonly prescribed.
rows.australia: Most don't need antibiotics. Treat with penicillin where acute rheumatic fever risk is high, e.g. many First Nations communities.

rows.india: Common, managed mainly surgically.
rows.australia: Very high rates in First Nations children, affecting hearing, speech and schooling. Ear health is a public health priority.

rows.india: Not universal at birth.
rows.australia: Universal newborn hearing screening in every state and territory.

rows.india: Declared eliminated as a public health problem.
rows.australia: Still endemic in some remote Aboriginal communities; controlled with the SAFE strategy (surgery, azithromycin, facial cleanliness, environment).

rows.india: Opportunistic, often at eye camps.
rows.australia: Regular retinal checks (usually every 1-2 years, more often in higher-risk and First Nations people), including retinal photography in general practice.

rows.india: Topical steroid-antibiotic drops are sometimes used empirically.
rows.australia: Don't start topical steroids without slit-lamp examination. Refer urgently for reduced vision, severe pain or suspected angle closure.

rows.india: No organised program; clinical breast examination is promoted.
rows.australia: BreastScreen Australia: free 2-yearly mammograms for women 50-74 (from 40 on request), no GP referral needed.

rows.india: Triple assessment.
rows.australia: Largely the same: triple assessment (clinical, imaging, biopsy). A normal mammogram alone doesn't exclude cancer.

rows.india: Younger women and later, often locally advanced disease.
rows.australia: Many cancers are screen-detected and early; breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy is common.

rows.india: Genetic testing limited by cost.
rows.australia: Assess familial risk category; refer to familial cancer services; BRCA testing is Medicare-funded for eligible people.

rows.india: Often a signed form with general risks, sometimes signed by family.
rows.australia: Rogers v Whitaker: disclose material risks, those a reasonable person or this patient would consider significant. Generic 'risks explained' isn't enough.

rows.india: Family members commonly interpret.
rows.australia: Use a professional interpreter (TIS National is free for doctors), not family, for consent.

rows.india: Focus on insulin and glucose control.
rows.australia: Stop SGLT2 inhibitors a few days before surgery because of euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk.

rows.india: Prolonged postoperative courses are common.
rows.australia: Single dose within 60 minutes before incision, usually cefazolin, per eTG.

rows.india: Oral and head-and-neck (tobacco chewing), cervical and breast cancer lead.
rows.australia: Prostate, breast, bowel, melanoma and lung lead. Bowel cancer rates are among the world's highest.

rows.india: No national program.
rows.australia: Free iFOBT every 2 years mailed at 50-74 (requestable from 45).

rows.india: No program.
rows.australia: National Lung Cancer Screening Program since July 2025: low-dose CT for high-risk current and former smokers aged 50-70.

rows.india: Oncologist or surgeon-led.
rows.australia: Multidisciplinary team meetings and Optimal Care Pathways, with the GP kept involved throughout.

rows.india: Obstetrician-led; government schemes promote institutional delivery.
rows.australia: GP shared care, midwifery care or obstetrician, public or private. Continuity of carer is valued.

rows.india: DIPSI single-step non-fasting 75 g test is common.
rows.australia: Fasting 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks (IADPSG criteria), earlier if high risk.

rows.india: Routine iron-folic acid and calcium for all, plus deworming.
rows.australia: Folic acid before conception (5 mg if high risk) and iodine 150 mcg. Iron only if deficient, not routinely.

rows.india: Td (tetanus-diphtheria) doses.
rows.australia: Pertussis (dTpa) at 20-32 weeks, influenza any trimester, and RSV vaccine in the third trimester.

rows.india: Tested once at booking.
rows.australia: Tested at booking, and many jurisdictions recommend repeat testing later in pregnancy due to outbreaks, especially in northern Australia.

rows.india: Oxytocin, misoprostol, uterotonics; blood availability can be a limit.
rows.australia: Largely the same approach: oxytocin, tranexamic acid, stepwise escalation, early senior help and massive transfusion protocol.

rows.india: Pritchard (IM) regimen is widely taught.
rows.australia: IV regimen: 4 g loading dose then 1 g per hour, with monitoring of reflexes, respiration and urine output.

rows.india: Anti-D often only after delivery or sensitising events.
rows.australia: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks, plus after birth and sensitising events.

rows.india: Referral to a higher centre.
rows.australia: Stabilise and arrange retrieval (e.g. RFDS); small hospitals may not have obstetric or theatre cover.

rows.india: Hospital birth promoted; high caesarean rates in private hospitals.
rows.australia: Hospital, birth centre or (uncommonly) home birth; midwife-led continuity models are common.

rows.india: Not routinely screened.
rows.australia: Screening at 35-37 weeks or a risk-based approach, depending on the hospital; intrapartum antibiotics if indicated.

rows.india: Repeat caesarean is often the default.
rows.australia: Planned VBAC is discussed and offered where suitable, as a shared decision.

rows.india: Family support during confinement; ASHA home visits.
rows.australia: Maternal and child health nurse visits, GP check at 6 weeks, and depression screening with the EPDS.

rows.india: Often diagnosed late, usually at laparoscopy.
rows.australia: National Action Plan and high awareness. Can be diagnosed clinically and on imaging, and treated empirically before surgery.

rows.india: Rotterdam criteria.
rows.australia: The international evidence-based PCOS guideline is led from Australia; know its lifestyle-first, whole-person approach.

rows.india: Genital TB is an important cause.
rows.australia: Genital TB is rare; think of it only in migrants from high-TB countries.

rows.india: Hormone therapy is used cautiously and less often.
rows.australia: Menopausal hormone therapy is generally supported for symptomatic women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, after individual risk assessment.

rows.india: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act (national), with gestation limits and doctor opinions.
rows.australia: State and territory law. Medical abortion (MS-2 Step) to 9 weeks can be prescribed in general practice. Objecting doctors must usually refer on.

rows.india: Female sterilisation dominates; also condoms, copper IUD, DMPA and centchroman.
rows.australia: LARCs (implant, hormonal IUD) are promoted as most effective. Centchroman is not available.

rows.india: Parental involvement is usually expected.
rows.australia: A Gillick-competent young person can consent to contraception confidentially.

rows.india: Commercial surrogacy banned; altruistic only.
rows.australia: Largely the same: only altruistic surrogacy is legal. Donor-conceived people can usually learn donor identity; rules vary by state.

rows.india: Syndromic management with pre-packed kits is common.
rows.australia: Test first (NAAT), treat per Australian STI Management Guidelines. Chlamydia: doxycycline 7 days. Gonorrhoea: ceftriaxone IM plus azithromycin.

rows.india: Endemic, tested at antenatal and STI clinics.
rows.australia: Ongoing outbreak among young First Nations people in northern and central Australia since 2011, with congenital cases. Low testing threshold.

rows.india: Testing mostly when symptomatic.
rows.australia: Offer asymptomatic testing to sexually active young people. Partner notification (contact tracing) is part of management.

rows.india: Government STI clinics.
rows.australia: Free public sexual health clinics, no Medicare card needed. PrEP is PBS-subsidised.

rows.india: Opportunistic Pap smear or VIA, usually from 30.
rows.australia: HPV test every 5 years, ages 25-74; self-collection is an option. Cytology only follows a positive HPV test.

rows.india: Cervical cancer is a leading cancer in women; HPV vaccination is being scaled up.
rows.australia: School-based program at 12-13 for all genders; aiming to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035.

rows.india: No screening.
rows.australia: Largely the same: no screening; CA-125 and ultrasound are not screening tests in average-risk women.

rows.india: Often D&C.
rows.australia: Transvaginal ultrasound first; endometrial thickness over 4 mm (or ongoing bleeding) needs endometrial sampling.

rows.india: BCG, OPV zero dose and hepatitis B birth dose.
rows.australia: Hepatitis B birth dose (ideally within 24 hours) and vitamin K. No routine BCG or oral polio.

rows.india: Not universal; varies by state and hospital.
rows.australia: Universal heel-prick bloodspot screening at 48-72 hours for many conditions, plus universal hearing screening.

rows.india: Bed-sharing is the norm.
rows.australia: Red Nose advice: baby on back, own safe cot, room-sharing not bed-sharing, face uncovered, smoke-free.

rows.india: Low birth weight, sepsis and hypothermia; kangaroo mother care.
rows.australia: Jaundice, prematurity and feeding problems. Breastfeeding promotion is largely the same.

rows.india: Mother-child protection card; checks at anganwadi.
rows.australia: State-issued personal health record (e.g. NSW 'Blue Book'); regular checks by maternal and child health nurses and GPs.

rows.india: WHO charts to 5 years, IAP charts after.
rows.australia: WHO charts to 2 years, then usually CDC charts.

rows.india: Undernutrition (SAM/MAM), stunting and anaemia.
rows.australia: Obesity is the common problem. Faltering growth needs investigation, including psychosocial factors.

rows.india: Food allergy is less of a focus.
rows.australia: Very high food allergy rates. ASCIA: introduce common allergens like peanut and egg around 6 months, in the first year.

rows.india: Dengue, malaria, typhoid, measles and TB.
rows.australia: Mostly imported. Focus on sepsis, meningitis, UTI and bronchiolitis. Measles is usually linked to travel.

rows.india: Nebulised salbutamol and antibiotics are common.
rows.australia: Supportive care only: no salbutamol, steroids or antibiotics. Oxygen and fluids as needed. Infant RSV immunisation programs exist.

rows.india: Treated as a skin problem.
rows.australia: In remote First Nations communities, treat impetigo and scabies (co-trimoxazole or benzathine penicillin) to prevent rheumatic fever and kidney disease.

rows.india: Clinical judgement and blood tests.
rows.australia: Largely the same: low threshold for a full septic workup under 3 months (RCH guidelines).

rows.india: Ponds and open water.
rows.australia: Leading cause of toddler death; pool fencing is law, active supervision emphasised.

rows.india: AHA or IAP algorithms.
rows.australia: ANZCOR guidelines and DRSABCD.

rows.india: Kerosene and pesticides.
rows.australia: Medicines, household products and button batteries (an emergency). Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26.

rows.india: Hospital adrenaline; autoinjectors uncommon.
rows.australia: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg; children at risk carry autoinjectors and ASCIA action plans at school.

rows.india: Routine at birth.
rows.australia: Not routine. Only for specific high-risk groups, e.g. some First Nations newborns and children travelling to high-TB countries.

rows.india: UIP: OPV plus fIPV, pentavalent, rotavirus, PCV, MR at 9 and 16-24 months, JE in endemic areas.
rows.australia: NIP: hexavalent (includes IPV), MMR at 12 months and MMRV at 18 months, meningococcal ACWY at 12 months. Check the Immunisation Handbook.

rows.india: Voluntary, with outreach.
rows.australia: 'No Jab, No Pay' family payments and 'No Jab, No Play' childcare rules in several states. Recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register.

rows.india: Not applicable.
rows.australia: Some extra funded vaccines, e.g. meningococcal B and extra pneumococcal doses; some vary by state.

rows.india: Psychiatrist prescribed; access varies.
rows.australia: Regulated by each state; often specialist initiation, permit or authority needed.

rows.india: Under-diagnosed.
rows.australia: Picked up on newborn screening; CFTR modulators are PBS-subsidised for eligible patients.

rows.india: Thalassaemia major needing chronic transfusion is common.
rows.australia: Uncommon; mainly in families from high-prevalence regions. Offer carrier testing in those groups.

rows.india: Insulin and finger-prick testing, often limited by cost.
rows.australia: Subsidised CGM and pumps are common; school care plans; NDSS support.

rows.india: POCSO requires reporting child sexual offences to police.
rows.australia: Mandatory reporting of reasonable suspicion of abuse or neglect to state child protection. Categories and thresholds vary by state.

rows.india: Taught mainly for sexual abuse.
rows.australia: Sentinel injuries matter: any bruise in a non-mobile infant needs assessment for abuse.

rows.india: Family is usually involved.
rows.australia: Parental consent isn't needed to report. Keep the child safe first; avoid confronting parents in a way that increases risk.

rows.india: Not applicable.
rows.australia: Be aware of the Stolen Generations and the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle, but culture never overrides a child's safety.

rows.india: Psychiatrist-led, often in hospital outpatients; Tele-MANAS helpline.
rows.australia: Mostly GP-led. A Mental Health Treatment Plan gives Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions (Better Access).

rows.india: Antidepressants are often the main treatment.
rows.australia: Psychological therapy first for mild to moderate depression; SSRIs added for moderate to severe.

rows.india: Few dedicated youth services.
rows.australia: headspace: free centres for 12-25 year olds.

rows.india: Tele-MANAS 14416.
rows.australia: Lifeline 13 11 14; Beyond Blue. Screening tools K10 and PHQ-9.

rows.india: Cannabis and alcohol.
rows.australia: Methamphetamine ('ice') is a major cause in emergency departments.

rows.india: Less emphasis.
rows.australia: Strong focus: regular metabolic monitoring on antipsychotics, because people with severe mental illness die years earlier from CVD.

rows.india: Family-centred care with hospital follow-up.
rows.australia: Community mental health teams with case managers; early psychosis services for young people.

rows.india: For treatment resistance.
rows.australia: Largely the same: after two failed antipsychotics, with mandated blood monitoring and myocarditis surveillance early on.

rows.india: CBT and SSRIs.
rows.australia: Largely the same: CBT and SSRIs first line.

rows.india: Often prescribed long term (e.g. clonazepam, alprazolam).
rows.australia: Short-term only. Alprazolam is Schedule 8 with restricted PBS listing.

rows.india: Limited psychologists; cost is a barrier.
rows.australia: GPs recommend free online CBT (MindSpot, THIS WAY UP) and Head to Health, plus Better Access sessions.

rows.india: Less often diagnosed.
rows.australia: Trauma-focused therapy first line (Phoenix Australia guidelines); common in refugees and veterans.

rows.india: General advice to cut down.
rows.australia: NHMRC: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and 4 in a day. A standard drink is 10 g alcohol.

rows.india: Smokeless tobacco and bidis are major concerns; e-cigarettes are banned.
rows.australia: Nicotine vapes are regulated medicines sold through pharmacies. Varenicline and NRT are PBS-subsidised; Quitline 13 7848.

rows.india: Needle exchange and OST through NACO programs.
rows.australia: Mainstream: needle and syringe programs, supervised injecting in Sydney and Melbourne, free take-home naloxone.

rows.india: Buprenorphine-based OST; methadone limited.
rows.australia: Methadone or buprenorphine (including long-acting injectables), often prescribed in general practice.

rows.india: Parents usually present and informed.
rows.australia: See the young person alone for part of the consult; HEADSS assessment. Confidentiality has limits for serious risk. Own Medicare card from 15.

rows.india: Few child psychiatry services.
rows.australia: headspace for 12-25 year olds; CAMHS for severe illness.

rows.india: Less often recognised.
rows.australia: Common exam theme. Medicare eating disorder plans; family-based treatment for adolescents; watch for medical instability.

rows.india: Assessed similarly.
rows.australia: Largely the same assessment, with collaborative safety planning and family involvement.

rows.india: Classify as low, medium or high risk.
rows.australia: Moving away from risk categories toward individualised assessment and safety planning.

rows.india: IM haloperidol with promethazine is common.
rows.australia: Verbal de-escalation, then oral medicine, then IM (e.g. droperidol, olanzapine, midazolam) per local guideline, with monitoring.

rows.india: Family usually brings the patient.
rows.australia: Police and ambulance have powers under state Mental Health Acts to take a person for assessment.

rows.india: Pesticides are a major method.
rows.australia: Ask about firearms and stockpiled medicines. Some states allow or require notifying police about firearms.

rows.india: Mental Healthcare Act 2017, national.
rows.australia: State and territory Mental Health Acts; terms and timeframes differ. Learn principles, not section numbers.

rows.india: Severe illness with risk or inability to care for self.
rows.australia: Mental illness, serious risk, treatment needed, and no less restrictive option. Independent tribunal review.

rows.india: Advance directives and nominated representatives.
rows.australia: Similar concepts (advance statements, nominated persons); availability and names vary by state.

rows.india: Unmodified ECT banned; restrictions for minors.
rows.australia: Involuntary ECT needs tribunal approval in most states; always given under anaesthesia.

rows.india: Used freely for agitation.
rows.australia: Non-drug approaches first. Risperidone is the only one PBS-subsidised for BPSD, limited to 12 weeks in Alzheimer's dementia.

rows.india: Not regulated in care homes.
rows.australia: Chemical and physical restraint in aged care are 'restrictive practices' needing consent, documentation and review.

rows.india: Recognised clinically.
rows.australia: Largely the same; screen with tools like the 4AT and find the cause.

rows.india: Family carers.
rows.australia: GP-led with memory clinic referral; Dementia Australia; plan capacity and substitute decision-making early.

rows.india: National Medical Commission.
rows.australia: AHPRA and the Medical Board of Australia; 'Good medical practice' code of conduct.

rows.india: Family often involved in decisions; written consent forms.
rows.australia: Competent adult decides (Rogers v Whitaker, material risk). Family don't consent for a competent adult.

rows.india: Passive euthanasia allowed with safeguards; active not.
rows.australia: Voluntary assisted dying is legal in every state under state law, with eligibility and waiting rules.

rows.india: Medico-legal cases go to police for inquest.
rows.australia: Unexpected, violent or unnatural deaths, and some others, are reported to the coroner; don't sign the death certificate.

rows.india: Standard biostatistics and study design.
rows.australia: Largely the same: sensitivity, NNT, bias and study types are examined identically.

rows.india: Census, NFHS, Sample Registration System.
rows.australia: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) and the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

rows.india: Infections alongside rising non-communicable disease.
rows.australia: Chronic disease, cancer, mental illness and ageing dominate.

rows.india: Gaps by region, caste and income.
rows.australia: The biggest gap is between First Nations and other Australians, e.g. life expectancy.

rows.india: Mostly opportunistic.
rows.australia: Organised population programs with invitations and registers (National Cancer Screening Register).

rows.india: Common cancers screened at NCD clinics.
rows.australia: Bowel (iFOBT 45-74), breast (mammogram 50-74), cervical (HPV every 5 years 25-74), lung (high-risk 50-70).

rows.india: No single guide.
rows.australia: RACGP 'Red Book' sets ages and intervals. First Nations people get an annual health check and some screening earlier.

rows.india: Tribal health has some parallels, but the history is different.
rows.australia: Colonisation, dispossession and the Stolen Generations drive today's health gaps. Closing the Gap sets national targets.

rows.india: Not applicable.
rows.australia: Ask every patient if they identify as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander; don't assume from appearance.

rows.india: Not applicable.
rows.australia: Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services; involve Aboriginal Health Workers or Practitioners; annual health check; PBS co-payment help.

rows.india: Doctor-led, often directive.
rows.australia: Cultural safety is judged by the patient. Involve family, allow time, avoid jargon, respect Sorry Business and gender-specific business.

rows.india: IDSP reporting to district surveillance units.
rows.australia: Report to the state or territory public health unit; the core list is national, but lists and timeframes vary by state.

rows.india: Similar public health duty.
rows.australia: Consent isn't needed to notify, but tell the patient you are doing it.

rows.india: Weekly and outbreak reporting.
rows.australia: Some (e.g. meningococcal disease, measles) need urgent phone notification on clinical suspicion, before lab confirmation.

rows.india: Health workers do field follow-up.
rows.australia: Public health units lead tracing and prophylaxis; the GP supports and handles STI partner notification.

rows.india: Largely out of pocket, with government hospitals and schemes like PM-JAY.
rows.australia: Universal Medicare covers public hospitals and subsidises GP and specialist care; optional private insurance.

rows.india: Patients can see specialists directly.
rows.australia: GP referral needed for Medicare-rebated specialist care. GPs are the gatekeepers; continuity is valued.

rows.india: Generic drugs and Jan Aushadhi stores.
rows.australia: Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme subsidises listed drugs with a co-payment and safety net.

rows.india: Doctors concentrated in cities.
rows.australia: Same problem; many overseas-trained doctors start rurally under Distribution Priority Area rules.

rows.india: Factories Act and ESI scheme.
rows.australia: Safe Work Australia and state regulators; state workers' compensation. GPs complete certificates of capacity focused on return to work.

rows.india: Silicosis, byssinosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis.
rows.australia: Silicosis from engineered stone (banned since July 2024), asbestos diseases, and re-emerged coal workers' pneumoconiosis in Queensland.

rows.india: Basic medical certificate.
rows.australia: Austroads standards, stricter for commercial drivers than private drivers.
